result.summary: Hera and Athena persuade Aphrodite (Cypris) to send Eros to make Medea love Jason. Jason leads a small party to Aeetes' palace, where Eros wounds Medea with his arrow and Argus explains the Argonauts' errand to the king.

scenes.title: Hera and Athena take counsel
scenes.summary: Hera and Athena discuss how Jason can win the fleece and decide to seek Cypris's help.
scenes.stakes: The Argonauts' quest fails without divine help against the overweening Aeetes.

scenes.title: The goddesses ask Cypris
scenes.summary: Hera and Athena visit Cypris and Hera asks her to make her son Eros inspire Medea's love for Jason. Cypris agrees reluctantly.
scenes.stakes: Hera's favourite Jason may fail and Pelias escape punishment.

scenes.title: Cypris bribes Eros
scenes.summary: Cypris finds Eros gambling with Ganymedes and promises him Zeus's golden ball if he strikes Medea. He takes his bow and flies down to earth.
scenes.stakes: Cypris risks being slighted by her defiant son.

scenes.title: Jason's plan and the Colchian plain
scenes.summary: Jason proposes to try words before force and chooses companions to go to Aeetes. They cross the plain where corpses hang from trees.
scenes.stakes: The crew's homecoming depends on Jason's approach to Aeetes.

scenes.title: Aeetes' palace and Chalciope
scenes.summary: Hera hides the party in mist. They admire the palace built by Hephaestus and meet Medea and Chalciope, who greets her sons.
scenes.stakes: The strangers are in the stronghold of a hostile king.

scenes.title: Eros shoots Medea
scenes.summary: Chalciope laments, and Eros unseen shoots Medea, who is consumed by love for Jason.
scenes.stakes: Medea is overcome by a love that will upend her loyalties.

scenes.title: Argus explains the errand
scenes.summary: At the banquet Aeetes questions his grandsons, and Argus describes the shipwreck, the Argonauts and Jason's lineage.
scenes.stakes: Argus must win Aeetes' goodwill for the quest without provoking him.

alias_notes.explanation: Cypris and Cytherea are cult titles of the goddess of love, Aphrodite.
The Colchians gave Apsyrtus this nickname, meaning shining, because he outshone the youths.

notable_quotes.reason: Jason prefers persuasion to force, a recurring theme of his leadership.
Memorable simile of a small brand kindling a great fire for Medea's love.

analysis.text: Love is imposed on Medea by divine design, turning the quest from a contest of strength into one of passion and persuasion.
The Colchian custom of hanging the dead in trees and the hospitality to strangers reflect Greek ideas of foreign lands and of xenia, protected by Zeus.

legacy.text: Apollonius's portrait of Medea's love, with its psychological detail, influenced Virgil's depiction of Dido in the Aeneid.

fun_facts.text: Book 3 opens with an invocation to Erato, the Muse whose name is linked to eros, love.

language_notes.text: Erato is the Muse of love poetry; the poet invokes her for help, as epic poets traditionally do at a new book's start.
Her name is tied to love because it resembles Eros, the Greek word for love.
"Made trial of" means tested or sounded out; Hera probes Athena's thoughts before revealing her own plan.
"Overweening" means arrogant and excessively proud; Aeetes is expected to resist persuasion.
"Accost" means to approach and speak to; "her son" is Eros, the god of love, whose arrows cause desire.
"A stranger to the darts of love" means Athena, a virgin goddess, has no experience of or part in desire.
Cypris is a name for Aphrodite, the goddess of love, linked to Cyprus. Her husband is Hephaestus, the lame smith god.
The floating island is a volcanic forge place; Hephaestus's smithy was often set in volcanic islands, fitting 'blast of flame'.
'Chief among goddesses' is a flattering address; Cypris teases that such powerful visitors rarely call on her.
Ixion was a mortal bound by Zeus to a wheel in the underworld as punishment. Hera means she would go to any extreme.
Hera, disguised as an old woman, tested whether men were respectful. Jason carried her across the river and lost a sandal, as the story goes.
Cytherea is another title of Aphrodite, from the island Cythera, where she was said to have landed or been worshipped.
"Dice" here translates a Greek word for knucklebones, small bones or similar pieces used in a children's game of chance.
"Unutterable rogue" means a rascal too bad for words; Cypris scolds Eros playfully.
Adrasteia was the nurse who helped hide the infant Zeus on Mount Ida in Crete (the Idaean cave) from his father Cronos.
"Zones" are the separate bands or sections of the ball's surface, each stitched with double seams.
Swearing by the heads of herself and Eros is a mother's oath, meant to reassure him that she will not cheat him.
A baldric is a belt worn over the shoulder to carry a quiver or sword.
"Aeson's son" is a patronymic for Jason, used instead of his name.
The syntax is compressed: Jason will try words first, to learn whether Aeetes will yield the fleece out of friendship or, trusting in his might, reject the quest.
"Frowardness" means stubborn, willful perversity; here, Aeetes' attitude and temper.
"I ween" is archaic for "I think" or "I suppose"; "catty" is likely a misprint for "carry".
Phrixus fled on the golden-fleeced ram from his stepmother Ino's plots and from being sacrificed by his father Athamas, and was welcomed by Aeetes.
"I wis" is archaic for "I know" or "certainly"; here it is a narrator's aside.
The sentence is obscure: men's bodies hang in the air, while women are buried in the earth, so earth and air share the dead equally.
Triglyphs are vertical grooved blocks in a Doric frieze; here they are bronze, with a stone coping (top course) resting on them.
The Pleiads are a star cluster; their setting (autumn) and rising (spring) marked the farming seasons, so the spring warms in winter and cools in summer.
Cytaean means of Cytaea (Cyte), a Colchian town; the poet uses it for Colchis generally.
The Phlegraean fight was the battle of the gods against the Giants; Helios rescued the wounded Hephaestus, hence the gift of the bulls and plough.
Phaethon means 'shining'; the name also recalls Helios' son Phaethon, who drove the sun's chariot.
'Was not wont to haunt' means she was not accustomed to frequent the palace.
Phrixus's sons were sent to Orchomenus in Boeotia to claim the inheritance of Athamas, Phrixus's father. Chalciope scornfully doubts the place is worth the journey.
Thralls are slaves or bondservants; billets are short pieces of cut wood used as fuel.
Breese is an old word for the gadfly, a biting fly that maddens cattle.
Aeson's son is Jason, identified by his father. The arrow-notch is the slot at the arrow's end, fitted to the bowstring.
Thralls are servants or slaves, here the household attendants who prepare the feast and baths.
The isle of Enyalius is the island of Ares (Enyalius is a war-god title), where the brothers were shipwrecked and found the Argonauts.
The birds of Ares were man-eating, feather-shooting birds on the island; Hercules and the Argonauts had driven them away.
"Bootless venture" means a useless or doomed undertaking; the king (Pelias) hopes Jason will die trying.
Phrixus fled on the golden ram and was later killed or lost; his unavenged spirit and the fleece are tied to the curse on Aeolus' line.
The Sauromatae were a people of the steppe north of the Black Sea, here named as enemies of Aeetes.
Augeias is a son of Helios by tradition, so he is Aeetes' kinsman; Telamon's descent from Zeus via Aeacus is also cited.

context_notes.text: Hera favours Jason and the Argonauts. They are hiding in the reeds near Colchis, where Aeetes keeps the golden fleece.
Cypris is Aphrodite, goddess of love, named for Cyprus. Medea, Aeetes' daughter, is a sorceress.
Athena was born from Zeus's head and remained a virgin goddess of wisdom and craft.
The Phasis is the river of Colchis, where King Aeetes keeps the Golden Fleece. The Argonauts have just arrived.
Pelias, king of Iolcus, had neglected Hera's worship and sent Jason after the fleece hoping he would die. Hence Hera's grudge.
Cypris's son is Eros (Love), whose arrows cause desire. Aeetes' daughter is Medea, a sorceress who can help Jason.
Cypris is another name for Aphrodite, goddess of love; Eros is her son. She wants Medea to fall in love with Jason.
Ganymedes was a beautiful Trojan boy carried off by Zeus to serve as cupbearer to the gods.
Hephaestus was the divine smith who made wondrous objects for the gods, so comparing the ball to his work is high praise.
Zeus, as protector of strangers and suppliants (Zeus Xenios), enforced the sacred duty of hospitality, which Jason relies on.
Hermes' wand is the herald's staff, the caduceus, which marked its bearer as a protected envoy.
The plain is named for Circe, Aeetes' sister in Greek myth, linking Colchis to the world of magic.
Hera favours Jason and protects the Argonauts, here by hiding them so they can reach Aeetes unnoticed.
Hephaestus is the divine smith and craftsman, who makes marvellous objects for gods and favoured kings.
Apsyrtus is Medea's half-brother; he will later die during the flight of the Argonauts.
Hecate is a goddess of magic, night and crossroads; Medea's priesthood foreshadows her skill in sorcery.
Aeetes is king of Colchis and father of Medea and Chalciope. Eidyia is his wife.
Eros is the god of love, here a winged archer whose arrows cause desire. Aeetes' palace is in Colchis, where the Argonauts have arrived.
Aeetes is king of Colchis. His daughter Chalciope married Phrixus, and her sons, including Argus, have returned with the Argonauts.
Circe, Aeetes' sister, was a daughter of Helios the sun-god and lived in the west, in Italy.
Pallas Athena helped design the Argo, the ship that carries the heroes.

literary_notes.text: The poet addresses the Muse directly, using the second person to ask for inspiration and to explain her link to love.
Hera poses alternatives, force-free scheme or persuasion, framing the problem the whole book will explore.
The plan to make Medea love Jason points to the central events of the book and its tragic consequences.
Cypris speaks 'crafty words', pretending not to know why the goddesses have come, so her teasing hides her shrewdness.
Cypris's stunned silence and awe show Hera's commanding status compared to the love goddess.
Eros is shown as a willful, defiant child, so the god of love resists even his mother, which adds humor.
The goddesses smile at the idea that Love troubles Love's own mother, an ironic joke on Cypris.
Eros is shown as greedy and gleeful with a flushed cheek, a mischievous child, which suits his power to cause trouble.
Cypris scolds Eros for cheating a child, yet she is about to bribe him to trick Medea, a far worse deception.
The ball is compared to a star as it streaks through the sky, stressing its marvelous, almost divine quality.
The sweeping view of earth, cities, rivers and ocean gives a vivid sense of Eros's flight down from Olympus.
Jason presents himself as a leader who invites free speech and shared responsibility, stressing the group's equality.
Speech "smoothing the path" treats persuasion as clearing a road, in contrast with the rough work of force.
The corpses hanging from the treetops give a grim, unsettling image and foreshadow the danger and strangeness of Colchis.
Fountains of milk, wine, oil and water give a vivid, abundant picture of the palace's marvellous richness.
The fire-breathing bronze bulls and adamant plough anticipate the task Aeetes will set Jason.
The mother's joy, raised hands and sobs make the reunion emotional and humanise the household.
Eros's disorienting, unseen approach is compared to a gadfly attacking cattle, suggesting love as a sudden, maddening sting.
The arrow is called a messenger of pain, foretelling that love will bring suffering to Medea.
The sweet pain that melts her soul joins pleasure and anguish, the central paradox of love.
A tiny brand setting twigs ablaze mirrors love growing secretly from a small spark into a consuming fire in Medea.
Argus speaks gently and cautiously, fearing for Jason, showing his tact and loyalty as he manages a dangerous host.
The curse tied to the fleece and Pelias' hidden hostility hint at the dangers the quest will bring.
Argus ends by stressing the heroes' divine descent, an appeal designed to win Aeetes' respect and soften his anger.
